source.title: Language Modeling by Language Models
source.authors: Junyan Cheng; Peter Clark; Kyle Richardson

record.tranche_reason: The study cites scaling laws as motivation for its Ladder-of-Scales verification budget, without testing the claim’s held-out-loss laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. It separately plots training-loss trends.
record.gate_note: The study reports training loss by parameter count and training tokens (Figures 46–47) and says the overall trend is downward. These are training-loss plots, not held-out loss, and the paper does not fit or report power laws, test predictions from smaller runs, or measure compute-optimal parameter/token splits. Its downstream benchmark comparisons and unit-based task-prediction results do not test the listed downstream-predictability version.
record.test_reason: The study uses scaling laws only to motivate its Ladder-of-Scales verification budget. Its one scaling-related result is a pair of figure-only plots of training loss against parameters (Fig. 46) and tokens (Fig. 47), described in one sentence as a downward trend. No held-out loss, power-law fit, extrapolation, compute-optimal split or shape-at-fixed-size comparison is reported. The downstream tables compare architectures at fixed scale, not performance as a function of scale.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but secondary. The paper's main conclusion is that Genesys, a multi-agent genetic-programming system, discovers LM architectures competitive with GPT2/Mamba2 (6/9 benchmarks at 350M). The scaling remark is an appendix aside that the training-loss trend shows 'most designs follow scaling laws'.
record.recipe_differences: The study runs architecture-discovery training and plots training-loss trends across its designs; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fits or compute-optimal analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Training loss decreases with parameter count and training tokens across the ~1,000 evolved designs at 14M–350M scale (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM-discovered architectures trained at 14M–350M parameters, training loss generally decreases with scale; no power-law fit or held-out loss is reported.

record.problems: The scaling-related evidence is presented only as plots, without extracted numeric values or fitted exponents. It concerns training loss rather than held-out loss, and the reported scales reach 14M–350M parameters rather than demonstrating extrapolation over orders of magnitude.

untested.parts: Held-out loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute; only unfitted training-loss trends are shown.
All parts; no predictions from small runs.
All parts; no compute-optimal allocation analysis.
All parts. The auto-tuner fixes a depth-first shape (citing Tang et al.), but the effect of shape is not measured.
Downstream performance is compared only between architectures at fixed scale (125M/25B, 350M/50B tokens), not as a function of scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The tranche is closer to T4/T6: scaling laws are a motivating heuristic for budget allocation (Ladder of Scales). The 125M vs 350M downstream tables (Tables 14 and 5) incidentally show higher averages at 350M, but these are not framed or analysed as scaling predictability.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss and whether it follows a power law when parameters, tokens, or compute vary.
Whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and departure from a single power law.
